Marit noticed it the way she noticed most things: late, and only because something had gone wrong. The bucket of mussels she'd left on the flat rock was already half-submerged, the rope she'd tied it with lifting and slackening like something breathing.

She checked the tide table pinned inside the shed door. High water, 14:12. Her watch said 13:09. The table had been right for forty years. Her father had used it. Her grandmother had used the one before it.

She waded out to the rock anyway, skirt hitched, and dragged the bucket back. The water was warmer than it should have been in October. That was the second wrong thing.

Back on the shingle she stood and looked at the bay. The sea was flat, grey, ordinary. Gulls on the breakwater. The ferry's smudge far out past the point, right on time. Everything behaving except the water itself, which kept coming, quiet and patient, up the beach and over the line of dried weed that marked where it was supposed to stop.

The lighthouse keeper's cottage had been empty since March. Marit had the key. She told herself she was going up there to check the barometer, which was true, and not to look at the old man's logbook, which was also true, and which she would do anyway.

Gorse on both sides, salt-stunted, still throwing out yellow in October as if it hadn't been told. Twice she stopped and looked back. The sea had not come any further than the shed. It lay against the doorstep like a dog that had been told to wait.

The key turned stiffly. Inside it smelled of cold ash and paraffin and, under that, him: pipe tobacco gone stale in the curtains. She didn't put the light on.

The barometer hung where it always had, beside the window that faced the point. She tapped the glass the way he'd taught her when she was nine. The needle didn't move. It sat at Fair, a little above Change, which was wrong for the sky she'd walked up under and wrong for a sea that was doing what it was doing.

The logbook was in the drawer of the table, under a tide table identical to hers. She knew before she opened it that she would read it. She sat down first, because her knees wanted her to.

His hand was small and tidy and got smaller as the entries went on. Dates, high water predicted, high water observed. For years the two columns matched. Then, from the previous autumn, they began to part. Four minutes. Nine. Twenty-two. He had underlined nothing. He had simply kept writing it down.

The last entry was the second of March. Observed: 51 minutes early. Beside it, in the margin, one word she had to tilt the page to read.
